trasitioning.title: Transitioning legacy applications to the cloud
trasitioning.author: Samuel Lincoln - July 26, 2025
trasitioning.description1: When transitioning legacy applications to the cloud, there are several critical factors to consider beyond just moving the code and data. It’s essential to plan carefully to ensure scalability, security, and business continuity throughout the process.
trasitioning.description2: A successful modernization typically involves multiple phases:
trasitioning.description3: where you analyze the current state, define objectives, and design the target environment with scalability and maintainability in mind;
trasitioning.description4: where migration and refactoring take place; and finally,
trasitioning.description5: where you secure, test and fine-tune the solution to meet performance and compliance requirements.
trasitioning.description6: In this article, I’ll outline these key steps and share practical strategies to help make the transition smooth and effective — while preserving the reliability and security that businesses depend on.
trasitioning.assessmentPlanningDescription1: The first step is to perform a thorough assessment of the existing application. This includes analyzing the architecture, identifying dependencies and bottlenecks, and reviewing security gaps and business-critical processes. It’s important to map out all functionalities, integrations, and flows of sensitive data, as well as to document potential risks and define the key business requirements that must be preserved during the migration.
trasitioning.assessmentPlanningDescription2: Next, it’s essential to define the modernization strategy itself: whether the application will be partially refactored, fully rewritten, or simply rehosted with minimal changes. Based on this decision, you can design the target architecture — for example, moving towards containerization, adopting microservices, or implementing serverless components — always aiming for scalability, maintainability and alignment with business goals.
trasitioning.assessmentPlanningDescription3: The third step focuses on security. Migrating from on-premises to the cloud requires clearly defined strategies for managing secrets and credentials, implementing data encryption in transit and at rest, and setting up robust authentication and authorization mechanisms. These measures are essential to protect sensitive information and to ensure compliance with industry standards and business requirements.
trasitioning.implementationDescription1: With the strategy and architecture defined, the next step is to implement the infrastructure. This should be done using Infrastructure as Code tools like Terraform, which make deployments repeatable and auditable. Depending on the application’s complexity and requirements, it may also be necessary to use orchestration tools such as Kubernetes or take advantage of managed cloud services to simplify scalability and maintenance.
trasitioning.implementationDescription2: The following step is to create an automated pipeline to streamline the build, testing, security scanning and deployment processes. Using tools like GitHub Actions, you can implement a robust CI/CD workflow that ensures new changes are consistently tested and securely deployed to production, reducing manual effort and the risk of human error.
trasitioning.validationOptimizationDescription1: Once the infrastructure is in place and the application is running in the cloud, the final step is validation and continuous optimization. This includes setting up monitoring, logging and auditing tools to track performance, usage patterns and potential security issues. These insights help identify bottlenecks or vulnerabilities early, allowing for ongoing improvements to ensure the system remains reliable, secure and efficient over time.
trasitioning.validationOptimizationDescription2: Lastly, it’s important to produce comprehensive technical documentation covering the architecture, processes and key decisions made during the migration. In parallel, the team should be prepared and trained to maintain and evolve the modernized solution, ensuring they are equipped to handle future updates and keep the system aligned with business needs.

microservices.title: Leveraging Microservices and Serverless Architectures on AWS
microservices.author: Samuel Lincoln - July 27, 2025
microservices.description1: Microservices architecture is an approach where an application is decomposed into a set of smaller, independent services, each responsible for a specific business capability. Instead of having a single, monolithic codebase and shared database, each microservice maintains its own code, database and lifecycle, which improves scalability and maintainability. In practice, applying this architecture means splitting the system along business domains to create loosely coupled services. Communication between them can happen through REST APIs — typically managed by an API Gateway — or via messaging systems such as Amazon SNS or SQS, which help to decouple services and add resilience to the overall architecture. This model also enables teams to work on different services independently, deploy them separately and scale only the parts of the system that actually need more capacity.
microservices.description3: "Serverless" is a cloud computing model where you write and deploy functions that run in response to events, without provisioning or managing servers directly. In this architecture, the cloud provider automatically handles scaling, availability and infrastructure maintenance. On AWS, serverless is most commonly implemented with services like AWS Lambda, which execute code on-demand when triggered by events such as API requests, file uploads or message queues. A practical way to use serverless alongside microservices is to run core services in containers, while offloading asynchronous or event-driven tasks — like background data processing or notifications — to serverless functions. This approach combines the flexibility and fine-grained scaling of serverless with the structure and control offered by containerized microservices.
microservices.description5: To ensure continuous monitoring and quickly detect issues, it’s important to implement centralized logging and observability across all services. In AWS, this can be done using CloudWatch to collect and aggregate logs, along with tools like Grafana to visualize key metrics in real time. Additionally, using AWS X-Ray to collect distributed traces helps identify performance bottlenecks and understand how requests flow through different microservices and serverless components. This end-to-end visibility is critical for maintaining reliability and optimizing the system over time.
microservices.description7: This design keeps each service independent and highly scalable, enabling the system to handle changes in demand with elasticity. By combining microservices and serverless components, and implementing centralized logging and tracing, the architecture maintains strong observability and resilience — ensuring the application remains robust, maintainable and ready to adapt to future business needs.

cicd.title: Implementing CI/CD Pipelines with Modern Tools
cicd.author: Samuel Lincoln - July 27, 2025
cicd.description1: In cloud projects, it’s essential to design a DevOps pipeline that enables frequent and reliable deployments without compromising security or stability. A well-structured pipeline supports automation, ensures traceability of changes and provides mechanisms for fast rollback when needed. This approach not only helps teams deliver updates quickly but also maintains the resilience and compliance required in modern cloud environments.
cicd.description3: To support continuous integration and deployment, specific pipelines should be built for each server or function, running multiple integration and unit tests, as well as performing static code analysis and security scanning. Tools such as Jenkins, GitLab CI/CD, or GitHub Actions can automate these workflows. For managing dependencies, building artifacts, and deploying changes with zero downtime, technologies like Docker, Terraform, Ansible, and Kubernetes help ensure automation, consistency, and high availability throughout the process.
cicd.description5: To ensure traceability, it is important to maintain consistent commit messages and adopt standardized branching and tagging strategies throughout the project. Additionally, deployment techniques like blue/green deployments and canary releases can be used to gradually introduce changes, allowing teams to identify and resolve potential issues before they affect the entire user base.
cicd.description7: To enable safe rollbacks, deployments should be made immutable, ensuring that the last known stable build remains readily available for immediate restoration in case of failures. Additionally, integrating centralized logging and monitoring helps track application health in real time and facilitates rapid identification of root causes when issues arise.

aiPostMortem.title: You can't blame ChatGPT in a post-mortem
aiPostMortem.subtitle: The role of artificial intelligence in infrastructure engineering and why technical knowledge still matters.
aiPostMortem.author: Samuel Lincoln
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence is already part of every stage of software development: it writes code, generates tests, reviews pull requests and even helps operate systems in production. Used the right way, it saves hours of work. But when the project involves critical infrastructure, the margin for error is much smaller.

Poorly written code usually charges a gradual price: slower response times, growing complexity, piling technical debt. It's bad, but usually contained. A mistake in infrastructure is a different story. A wrong permission, a badly written policy or a command run without review can take down an entire service at once, with direct impact on customers and on revenue.

AI models may be able to design and implement architectures and servers, but they can't be held accountable when something goes wrong. In practice, the responsibility for a bad decision or a model hallucination falls on whoever accepted it, not on OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or any of the others. That's why behind any AI there has to be a competent professional who understands what is being done.

Because AI makes everything easier and faster, it's not unusual to see good professionals giving in to the temptation of accepting suggestions and implementations without properly reviewing them. After all, AI is usually right. Usually. But what happens when the unexpected occurs? When the model doesn't grasp the full context of the application and touches something it shouldn't? When it makes a serious mistake? At that point, someone who doesn't understand what was done can turn a medium-severity incident into a catastrophe.

I use AI a lot in my day-to-day work, and it saves me hours. Today it helps me build observability dashboards, read and extract information from large volumes of logs, analyze errors and write post-mortems. During an incident, for example, I need to cross-reference logs from applications, databases and queues to understand what happened and in what order. Doing that “the old-fashioned way” would take hours, sometimes days, of manual reading and correlation. Now, with an agent organizing and summarizing that data, I reach my first hypotheses within a few hours and spend my time on what really matters: deciding which one makes sense and what to do about it.

That division is where the real gain lies. AI is very good at processing volume: reading thousands of log lines, finding patterns, putting together the first version of a dashboard or an incident timeline. But it doesn't know what's normal in my environment, which services are critical or what changed last week. That context is mine, and it's what separates a plausible hypothesis from the actual root cause.

AI also helps me think about architecture. I describe the problem and it brings ideas, alternatives and paths I might not have considered at first. When I need to run something on AWS, it gives me the exact commands, and I no longer have to open the documentation at every step. It's also good for weighing a decision: asking for the pros and cons of an idea helps me see risks and costs before I start. But I'm the one who decides. I read every command it suggests before running it, check what it does, which resource it touches and what happens if it goes wrong, and review everything carefully. My rule is simple: AI can read, but it can't change anything. It queries logs, metrics and configurations freely, and that's what makes an agent so useful during an incident. But anything that changes the environment, like applying a policy, modifying a resource or running a deploy, goes through me first, because a single dangerous or poorly thought-out command is all it takes to become a problem in production.

Over the past year running a production infrastructure, I've found mistakes in the suggestions of the most advanced models many times. In some cases the idea was good, but it didn't fit the application's context and would have caused problems if implemented the way the model designed it. In others, it hallucinated: it stated something I noticed was wrong and, when I questioned it, corrected itself.

But notice what happened: the model only corrected itself because I questioned it, and I only questioned it because I knew the answer was wrong. The problem is that it would have given in just the same if I had been the one who was wrong. Most models tend to agree with whoever they're talking to: if you challenge an answer, even with flawed arguments, the model will usually reconsider what it said and give in, whether you're right or not. That makes it very easy to “bend” the AI until it agrees with your point of view.

And that's the risk: you keep pushing until the model validates an idea you already wanted approved, and that validation starts to look like a second technical opinion, when it's really just your own confirmation bias coming back at you. It gets worse when it turns into an argument. “The AI agreed with me” gets used to defend a proposal in a technical discussion, and a weak idea takes on the air of a validated one. An AI that gave in to your insistence hasn't confirmed that you're right. And if the decision goes wrong, “the AI agreed with me” won't make it into the post-mortem as the root cause.

At the end of the day, nothing replaces technical knowledge gained through study and experience. AI is an incredibly powerful tool, it's here to stay and it's changing the way we build software, but I believe it's crucial that we keep the habit of studying and understanding what we do, even when AI could do it for us. That knowledge is what lets me notice when a suggestion doesn't apply to my context, when the model has hallucinated and when I'm just trying to get it to agree with me. Without it, I wouldn't even know the answer was wrong.

At the end of 2021, the general public had no idea what an LLM was. ChatGPT didn't exist yet, and GPT-3, available only through an API, was far behind today's models. Today they work with contexts of millions of tokens, design systems, and write, review and test code at a level that impresses even experienced professionals. By 2031, models will be better and will probably make fewer mistakes. Even so, when something goes wrong in production, someone will have to explain what happened, why it was done and how to fix it. That person will be a valuable professional, and I want to keep being one who understands what they're doing.

aiPostMortem.quote2: An AI that gave in to your insistence hasn't confirmed that you're right.
